clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene, impairing thymic negative selection and permitting escape of autoreactive T cells.
Classic diagnostic triad is chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism and autoimmune adrenal (Addisonian) insufficiency; two of three confirm the diagnosis.
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is usually the earliest manifestation, often appearing in infancy or early childhood.
Hypoparathyroidism typically precedes adrenal failure, and components accrue over years so lifelong surveillance is essential.
High-titre neutralising autoantibodies against type I interferons are almost universal and can be used as a diagnostic marker.
Autoantibodies to interleukin-17 and interleukin-22 correlate with the chronic candidiasis.
Additional features include hypogonadism, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, autoimmune hepatitis, enamel hypoplasia, nail dystrophy and keratoconjunctivitis.
Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive, with notable founder populations among Finns, Sardinians and Iranian Jews.
reference.pathophysiology: APECED arises from loss-of-function mutations in AIRE, a transcriptional regulator expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells. AIRE drives promiscuous expression of tissue-restricted self-antigens within the thymus, allowing developing T cells that recognise these antigens to be deleted or diverted to regulatory lineages. When AIRE is defective, this central tolerance fails, and autoreactive T cells escape to the periphery where they mount organ-specific autoimmune attacks against multiple endocrine and non-endocrine tissues. Neutralising autoantibodies to type I interferons and to Th17 cytokines further explain the susceptibility to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. The result is progressive, multi-organ autoimmunity accumulating throughout life.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis due to STAT1 gain-of-function mutation
additionalInvestigations: AIRE gene sequencing for confirmatory diagnosis
Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone
Short synacthen test with adrenocorticotrophic hormone and plasma renin/aldosterone
Organ-specific autoantibodies (21-hydroxylase, glutamic acid decarboxylase, intrinsic factor, hepatic)
Fasting glucose, thyroid function and gonadal hormone profile
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm or seizures
Development of oral or oesophageal squamous carcinoma complicating chronic candidiasis
Autoimmune enteropathy or intestinal dysfunction causing severe malabsorption
reference.prognosis: With hormone replacement and antifungal management most patients survive into adulthood, but mortality is raised by unrecognised adrenal crisis, hypocalcaemia, fulminant hepatitis and oral carcinoma. Lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance is required because new components continue to emerge.
pitfalls: Diagnosing isolated Addison disease or hypoparathyroidism without recognising the wider syndrome.
Failing to anticipate and screen for additional autoimmune components as they evolve over time.
Missing life-threatening adrenal insufficiency in a child already labelled with candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism.
Not counselling about surveillance for oral squamous carcinoma in long-standing mucocutaneous candidiasis.
Overlooking neutralising anti-interferon antibodies as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker.
references: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology, current edition
International Union of Immunological Societies phenotypic classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for autoimmune adrenal (Addisonian) insufficiency, with stress-dose escalation during illness, surgery or trauma
Correct autoimmune hypoparathyroidism with activated vitamin D analogues (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) plus calcium, monitoring for hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis
Suppress chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with azole antifungals, rotating agents and reviewing for azole resistance

Replace further endocrine axes as they fail — levothyroxine for autoimmune hypothyroidism, insulin for autoimmune diabetes, sex-steroid replacement for gonadal failure — and treat autoimmune hepatitis with corticosteroid-based immunosuppression such as azathioprine
Lifelong multisystem surveillance for newly emerging autoimmune components, with periodic endocrine, hepatic and haematological screening
Educate the family on adrenal-crisis recognition, provide an emergency parenteral hydrocortisone kit, and surveil the oral mucosa for squamous carcinoma given chronic candidiasis
Coordinate care through clinical immunology and endocrinology with dietetic and dental input
Offer genetic counselling and AIRE testing for siblings and family, reflecting autosomal recessive inheritance
